decision.quote: Numerous developmental studies of predominantly urban Western middle-class children suggest that children reach this milestone by 18 to 24 months of age. By 18 months, approximately 50% pass and by 24 months a significant majority of children (more than 70%) are reported to self- refer by touching or removing a mark from their own body (face or other body region) while exploring their mirror image (Amsterdam, 1972; Asendorpf, Warkentin, & Baudonnière, 1996; Bard, Todd, Bernier, Love, & Leavens, 2006; Bertenthal & Fisher, 1978; Lewis & Brooks-Gunn, 1979; Lewis & Ramsay, 2004; Nielsen, Dissanayake, & Kashima, 2003; Schulman & Kaplowitz, 1976). Here we report cross-cultural observations on the emergence of mirror self-recognition (MSR), using a simplified mark test, raising questions regarding the meaning and universal validity of this test as an ontogenetic benchmark of self-concept.
decision.reason: Addressing the prior scope objection: although the abstract and introduction frame the study as replicating the Western 18-to-24-month mirror self-recognition (MSR) milestone across cultures, Asendorpf, Warkentin, & Baudonnière (1996) appears only once in an eight-citation introductory literature cluster summarizing the general developmental milestone. When the authors operationalize the actual empirical benchmark tested in their one-tailed binomial analysis (Method, p. 4) and directly compare their empirical results against prior Western findings (Results, p. 5; General Discussion, pp. 8–9), they cite only Amsterdam (1972; retained in shipped row input_row_index 843), Bertenthal & Fisher (1978; target_index 3), Lewis & Brooks-Gunn (1979; target_index 4), and Lewis & Ramsay (2004; target_index 5). No specific empirical finding from Asendorpf et al. (1996) is ever stated, statistically tested, or compared with the results of Experiments 1 or 2.

decision.quote: In 2006, Bard et al. compared spontaneous and prompted self-orienting behaviors of children in the mark test and reported that maternal prompt- ing increased self-referential verbal labeling. Although no statistical tests were applied (n = 4), these findings do suggest that verbal prompts may be needed to encourage self-referential behav- ior and labeling (Bard et al., 2006).

decision.quote: The first experiment shows that only 2 out of 82 18- to 72-month-old Kenyan children manifested self-oriented behaviors toward the mark, most of them freezing while staring at their specular image.
